name: Potato
environment: Outdoor beds or large grow bags
water: Even moisture while tubers form; never waterlogged.
containerDepth: Use a large deep grow bag or container suitable for potatoes, with drainage and room to hill developing tubers; follow the chosen variety and container guidance.
problems: Colorado potato beetle, scab, late blight, poor drainage. Tubers exposed to light turn green.
calories: Meaningful calories per square foot compared with greens, but harvests vary widely; a small patch supplements stored food, it does not replace it.
start: Certified disease-free seed potatoes (not grocery potatoes). Small tubers whole; larger ones cut into ~1¼-inch pieces with 1–3 eyes, dried a few days at 60–70°F before planting.
soilTemp: Plant as soon as the soil warms and can be worked; emerged leaves can be damaged by frost — cover them if frost is forecast.
spacing: 10–12 in apart, 3–5 in deep, rows 30–36 in. Hill soil 6–8 in up the stems over the season.
medium: Loose, well-drained soil; potting mix in bags.
container: Grow bags work; keep adding mix over stems so tubers stay dark.
seedLife: Seed tubers are not stored like seed; buy certified seed each spring.
varieties: Choose early, mid and late varieties from certified seed suppliers; no single variety is endorsed here.
limits: New potatoes about 7–8 weeks after planting; full-size tubers when vines die back. Cure 10+ days at 60–65°F in the dark, then store cool (32–40°F, humid). Never eat green tubers or sprouts.
harvestStage: New potatoes can be earlier; mature storage potatoes need skin set and suitable curing. Never eat green or bitter tubers or plant foliage.

name: Dry beans (for storage)
water: Moderate; let pods dry on the plant late in the season.
containerDepth: 8 in+ (bean guidance); yields from containers are small.
problems: Killed by frost; needs a long enough warm season to dry down — challenging in the U.P. and cold inland sites. Wet fall weather can mold pods.
calories: Dried beans are protein- and energy-dense and store well, but each plant yields little; plan on a supplement only.
start: Direct seed after frost danger when soil is warm.
soilTemp: Wait until frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least about 60°F for planting. Cold, wet soil slows emergence and can rot seed; follow the packet and stable local weather.
spacing: Follow the packet; bush types fit small beds.
seedLife: About 3 year(s) under ideal cool, dry storage (Iowa State); viability declines over time. Rotate and test before relying on old packets.
varieties: Short-season dry bean varieties are preferred for northern sites; check days to maturity against your frost window.
limits: Days to maturity on the packet are from sowing; drying time adds more. Harvest before hard frost and finish drying indoors.

sources.title: How to store seeds and test germination rates

harvestStage: Fully mature dry seed, not young snap pods; dry thoroughly and cook correctly before eating. Never substitute raw dry beans into a canned-bean recipe.

name: Winter squash
containerDepth: 12–18 in and 5+ gallons (squash container guidance); vines sprawl.
problems: Squash vine borer, squash bugs, powdery mildew. Killed by frost; a short season may not ripen fruit.
calories: Moderate energy, excellent keeping vegetable when cured and stored cool and dry.
start: Direct seed after frost when soil is warm (or careful short-lived transplants).
soilTemp: Wait until frost danger has passed and soil is at least about 65°F for direct sowing. Warmer soil improves establishment; follow the variety and local weather.
spacing: Large: vines need several feet; bush types are smaller.
container: Only compact bush types; large containers.
seedLife: About 4 year(s) under ideal cool, dry storage (Iowa State); viability declines over time. Rotate and test before relying on old packets.
varieties: Prefer short-season types for the U.P. and cold inland areas; check days to maturity.
limits: Maturity is from sowing. Harvest before frost; cure and store cool and dry.

sources.title: New Michigan gardening calendar resources support home gardeners
How to store seeds and test germination rates

harvestStage: Mature winter squash with a firm rind; cultivar, curing and storage change keeping quality.

name: Peas
water: Even moisture; peas stall in heat.
containerDepth: 8 in deep; at least 2 gallons; trellis for vining types.
problems: Stops flowering above ~85°F (often by late June); cutworms, aphids, powdery mildew, root rot.
calories: Moderate; shelled peas add some protein and energy. Snap/snow peas are mostly a vegetable.
start: Direct seed as soon as the soil has thawed and can be worked.
soilTemp: Can be direct-seeded at 40–50°F soil; seedlings tolerate light frost, but flowers and pods can be damaged.
spacing: About 1 in deep; follow the packet for row spacing. Tall vining types need a trellis.
medium: Well-drained soil; potting mix in containers.
indoor: Pea shoots (young tops) can be grown in a sunny window or under lights, but they give greens, not a pea crop.
seedLife: About 3 year(s) under ideal cool, dry storage (Iowa State); viability declines over time. Rotate and test before relying on old packets.
varieties: Pick by type (shelling, snap, snow) and disease resistance; seed catalogs mark powdery-mildew resistant varieties.
limits: About 60 days from sowing in spring; midsummer sowings take longer (70–80 days) and may struggle in heat.

sources.title: Planting vegetables in midsummer for fall harvest
How to store seeds and test germination rates

harvestStage: Edible pods or fresh peas, depending on variety; fall crops typically take longer than spring crops.

name: Kale
containerDepth: 10 in deep and about 5 gallons per plant.
problems: Cabbage worms, flea beetles, aphids. Bitter or tough in heat.
calories: Low calories; valuable for vitamins and variety.
soilTemp: Cool soils are fine; among the hardiest — UMN lists kale as surviving down to about 20°F.
indoor: Baby leaves can grow under lights (12–16 h/day); full plants need a large container.
seedLife: Store cool and dry; test older seed.
varieties: Most kale varieties are cold hardy; choose by leaf type.
limits: Pick outer leaves repeatedly. Flavor often improves after light frost.

sources.title: Planting vegetables in midsummer for fall harvest

harvestStage: Usable leaves; baby leaves can be harvested before full maturity.

name: Cabbage
water: Even moisture; uneven watering splits heads.
containerDepth: 10 in deep and about 5 gallons per plant.
problems: Cabbage worms and loopers, root maggots, split heads.
calories: Low to moderate; stores for weeks in a cold place.
start: Start indoors about 4–6 weeks before transplanting, or buy healthy transplants. Planner default: 6 weeks; packet and local conditions take priority.
soilTemp: Tolerates cool soil; UMN lists cabbage as surviving to about 20°F.
indoor: Seedlings only; heads need outdoor space.
seedLife: About 5 year(s) under ideal cool, dry storage (Iowa State); viability declines over time. Rotate and test before relying on old packets.
varieties: Early varieties suit short seasons; storage types take longer.
limits: Days are from transplanting; early types ~50–60 days, storage types up to ~90.

sources.title: Planting vegetables in midsummer for fall harvest
How to store seeds and test germination rates

harvestStage: Marketable head, counted from outdoor transplanting; seedling-growing time is additional.

name: Spinach
problems: Bolts (goes to seed) quickly in long, warm days.
start: Direct seed early in spring or late summer.
spacing: Follow the packet; thin to give leaves room.
indoor: Possible for baby leaves under lights.
seedLife: About 5 year(s) under ideal cool, dry storage (Iowa State); viability declines over time. Rotate and test before relying on old packets.
varieties: Slow-bolting varieties help with spring plantings.
limits: Survives light frost and may overwinter with protection.

sources.title: Planting vegetables in midsummer for fall harvest
How to store seeds and test germination rates

harvestStage: Usable leaves; baby and full-size harvests differ.

name: Radishes
problems: Woody or hot roots in heat or dry soil; root maggots; flea beetles.
calories: Very low; fast and encouraging for beginners.
start: Direct sowing is recommended for root quality; follow the variety instructions.
spacing: Thin to about 1–2 in apart; sow small batches every 1–2 weeks.
indoor: Possible in a deep tray under strong light, but leggy in weak window light.
seedLife: About 5 year(s) under ideal cool, dry storage (Iowa State); viability declines over time. Rotate and test before relying on old packets.
varieties: Spring (small, fast) vs winter (large, slow) radishes differ greatly in days to harvest.
limits: Spring types ~25–30 days; larger winter radishes much longer. Can be dug until the ground freezes.

sources.title: Planting vegetables in midsummer for fall harvest
How to store seeds and test germination rates

harvestStage: Edible root; small spring and larger winter varieties mature at different rates.

name: Carrots
water: Keep the seedbed moist until sprouts appear (slow to germinate).
containerDepth: 12 in deep; thin to 2–3 in apart.
problems: Slow, uneven germination in crusted or dry soil; forked roots in rocky soil.
calories: Low to moderate; stores well cold and humid.
start: Direct sowing is recommended to avoid root disturbance and misshapen storage roots.
soilTemp: Cool soil; sow from early spring through early summer.
medium: Loose, stone-free soil or deep potting mix.
indoor: Not practical (deep containers, strong light, long season).
seedLife: About 3 year(s) under ideal cool, dry storage (Iowa State); viability declines over time. Rotate and test before relying on old packets.
varieties: Short or round types suit containers and heavy soils.
limits: Days are typical seed-packet values from sowing; check your packet.

sources.title: How to store seeds and test germination rates

harvestStage: Usable roots; baby and storage-root harvests differ.

name: Beets
containerDepth: 8 in deep; thin greens to 3 in.
problems: Poor germination in crusted soil; each 'seed' is a cluster, so thinning is needed.
calories: Moderate for a vegetable; greens are edible too.
seedLife: About 4 year(s) under ideal cool, dry storage (Iowa State); viability declines over time. Rotate and test before relying on old packets.
varieties: Choose by color and storage type.

sources.title: Planting vegetables in midsummer for fall harvest
How to store seeds and test germination rates

harvestStage: Edible roots; tender leaves can be ready sooner.

name: Leaf lettuce
environment: Indoor under lights or bright window; outdoor; containers
light: Bright, sustained light; supplemental lighting may be needed indoors in winter. Follow fixture guidance.
containerDepth: 4–8 in deep, at least 2 gallons; thin to ~9 in for full heads.
problems: Bitter and bolting in heat; leggy in weak light; damping-off in cold wet mix.
calories: Very low calories; fresh greens for morale and nutrients.
start: Direct sow leaf lettuce. Optional transplants can be started indoors about 3–5 weeks before planting out; follow variety and packet instructions.
soilTemp: Direct seed at 40–50°F soil; survives light frost.
medium: Potting mix (not garden soil) in containers.
indoor: One of the best indoor crops: Illinois Extension reports leaf lettuce ready in about 4 weeks under good light. Keep rooms 70°F or cooler.
container: Excellent in window boxes and shallow containers.
seedLife: About 5 year(s) under ideal cool, dry storage (Iowa State); viability declines over time. Rotate and test before relying on old packets.
varieties: Loose-leaf types are fastest and most forgiving indoors.
limits: Indoor lettuce needs adequate light intensity and a regular dark period. Set duration and distance for the crop and specific fixture; follow its instructions and adjust if growth is weak or leaves scorch. Windowsill yields remain limited.

sources.title: Grow Herbs and Lettuce Indoors this Winter
Planting vegetables in midsummer for fall harvest

harvestStage: Leaf or baby-leaf harvest, not a promise for mature heading types.

name: Swiss chard
calories: Low calories; harvest leaves for months.
soilTemp: Plant in early spring once soil is workable.
seedLife: Store cool and dry; test older seed.
varieties: Choose by stem color; all grow similarly.
limits: Cut outer leaves; plants keep producing through summer.
harvestStage: Usable leaves; small outer leaves can be harvested earlier.

name: Onions & green onions
water: Even moisture; stop watering as bulbs mature.
problems: Bulb size depends on day length variety; weeds compete strongly.
calories: Low; mainly flavor. Cured bulbs store well.
start: Plant sets or transplants outdoors in early spring. For seed-grown transplants, start indoors about 10–12 weeks ahead; planner default 11. Choose suitable long-day bulb varieties for Michigan.
indoor: Green onions regrow in a sunny window, giving small amounts.
container: Green onions do well in small containers.
seedLife: About 1 year(s) under ideal cool, dry storage (Iowa State); viability declines over time. Rotate and test before relying on old packets.
varieties: Choose long-day onion varieties for Michigan latitudes.
limits: Green onions in weeks; storage bulbs need the full season and curing.

sources.title: How to store seeds and test germination rates

harvestStage: Approximate harvest after sets or transplants are planted outdoors; green onions and cured storage bulbs differ. Seed-starting time is additional.

name: Bush snap beans
containerDepth: 8 in deep (12–18 in and 5 gal for best yields).
problems: Killed by frost; rot in cold wet soil; bean beetles.
calories: Low to moderate; a productive vegetable, not a staple.
soilTemp: Wait until frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least about 60°F for planting. Cold, wet soil slows emergence and can rot seed; follow the packet and stable local weather.
seedLife: About 3 year(s) under ideal cool, dry storage (Iowa State); viability declines over time. Rotate and test before relying on old packets.
varieties: Bush types mature faster than pole types.
limits: Beans are warm-season: unlike peas, they cannot go in early. Pick often to keep plants producing.

sources.title: Planting vegetables in midsummer for fall harvest
How to store seeds and test germination rates

harvestStage: Tender bush snap-bean pods, not fully dry seed or every pole-bean variety.

name: Tomatoes
water: Deep, even watering; containers may need daily water in heat.
containerDepth: For large plants, at least about 5 gallons and 12–18 inches deep; match variety and support, with drainage.
problems: Cold injury, late blight, blossom-end rot from uneven watering, short seasons in the U.P.
calories: Low calories; valuable fresh or preserved.
start: Start indoors 5–6 weeks before transplanting, or buy plants; harden off 1–2 weeks.
soilTemp: Plant after frost danger; MSU notes warm-season crops establish best in soil 75°F+. U.P. gardeners often wait until early–mid June.
indoor: Indoor fruiting needs very strong light and a large pot; not practical in an outage.
container: Choose a compact patio or determinate variety and its recommended pot size. Large tomato plants generally need at least a 5-gallon, 12–18-inch-deep container; larger volumes are easier to keep evenly watered. Tiny pots sharply limit growth.
seedLife: About 4 year(s) under ideal cool, dry storage (Iowa State); viability declines over time. Rotate and test before relying on old packets.
varieties: Short-season, determinate varieties for northern sites and containers.

sources.title: New Michigan gardening calendar resources support home gardeners
How to store seeds and test germination rates

harvestStage: First ripe fruits after transplanting; season and cultivar alter timing.

name: Peppers
containerDepth: 12–18 in deep and at least 5 gallons.
problems: Slow in cool weather; leggy seedlings in poor light.
start: Start indoors about 6–8 weeks before transplanting, with suitable light and warmth. Planner default: 8 weeks; follow variety instructions.
soilTemp: Plant after nights stay warm; warm-season soil 75°F+ ideal (MSU).
indoor: Seedlings only; fruiting indoors needs strong light.
container: Compact varieties do well in pots.
seedLife: About 2 year(s) under ideal cool, dry storage (Iowa State); viability declines over time. Rotate and test before relying on old packets.
varieties: Compact, short-season types for containers and northern sites.

sources.title: New Michigan gardening calendar resources support home gardeners
How to store seeds and test germination rates

harvestStage: Green versus fully colored fruit have different maturity times, counted from transplanting.

name: Basil
environment: Indoor sunny window or lights; outdoor after frost; containers
light: 6–8 h bright light; or 14–16 h under lights.
water: Let the surface dry slightly; drain well.
problems: Chilling injury below about 50°F, downy mildew, cold drafts by windows.
start: Transplants (or seed) — set outdoors only after frost danger (UMN: mid-to-late May in Minnesota).
indoor: Grows indoors with bright light; keep away from cold glass in winter.
seedLife: Store cool and dry; test older seed.
varieties: Any culinary basil; compact types suit windowsills.

sources.title: Grow Herbs and Lettuce Indoors this Winter

harvestStage: Usable leaves from sowing; transplants can be harvested earlier once established.

name: Parsley
light: Part sun to sun; 6–8 h indoors or under lights.
start: Transplants are easiest; seed is very slow to sprout.
soilTemp: Cool soil; can go out in early spring (UMN: mid-April in Minnesota).
indoor: Listed by Illinois Extension among herbs that do well indoors.
seedLife: Keep seed cool and dry; test older packets. Useful storage life varies, so the packet and a representative germination test matter more than a universal herb expiry.
varieties: Flat or curly — both grow similarly.

sources.title: Grow Herbs and Lettuce Indoors this Winter

sources.organization: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
sources.title: Parsley

harvestStage: Usable leaves from seed is a broad estimate; germination is slow and cultivar-specific. Transplants shorten the wait.

name: Chives
start: Divisions or transplants are fastest; seed is slow.
soilTemp: Cool soil; perennial outdoors in Michigan.
indoor: Illinois Extension lists chives among herbs that grow indoors.
seedLife: Keep seed cool and dry; test older packets. Do not infer a chive seed guarantee from a general onion-family rule.
limits: Cut leaves to an inch or two above the soil; regrows.

sources.title: Grow Herbs and Lettuce Indoors this Winter

harvestStage: Earliest light cutting from seed can begin around 60 days; established transplants or divisions are earlier.
